vignette:
He is a 49-year-old European man who has spent most of his adult life in fashion, moving between sketches, fittings, and deadlines with a practiced eye for detail. Before the trauma, he describes himself as energetic and exacting, someone who could lose himself for hours in fabric samples and color palettes. He and his wife have been married for many years, and their life together has generally been stable, built around work, travel, and the ordinary routines of a long relationship.

That changed when his wife was suddenly and seriously harmed. He tells the story in fragments, as if the event still refuses to settle into a single shape in his mind. One moment there was an ordinary day, and then there was panic, emergency calls, fluorescent hospital lighting, and the awful realization that someone he loves was not safe. He remembers the sound of his own voice sounding strange to him, too loud and too thin. He remembers waiting for updates, watching people move with purpose while he felt frozen. In the weeks after, he alternates between vivid images of what happened and gaps he cannot quite account for, as though his mind keeps approaching the memory and then pulling away.

Since then, he lives as if part of him remains at the scene, still braced for the next bad call. He is on edge from the moment he wakes. Small sounds startle him badly: a phone vibrating on a table, a door closing in the apartment building, a sudden siren outside his studio. He feels his body react before he can think, shoulders tightening, stomach dropping, heart racing. He checks on his wife repeatedly, sometimes calling or texting when he knows she is only in the next room. He says he hates how often he needs reassurance, but the fear is immediate and physical, not something he can reason away.

At night, the event returns in dreams and in flashes that come without warning. He can be looking at a rack of clothing or choosing thread color and suddenly he is back in the hospital corridor or in the moment he first understood how serious the injury was. He feels it in his body as if it is happening again: the coldness in his hands, the pressure behind his eyes, the urge to pace. He avoids anything that reminds him of the trauma. He has stopped driving the route to the hospital. He keeps away from certain news stories and from friends who ask detailed questions, because he cannot bear to retell it. Even at work, where he once enjoyed the social intensity of fashion shows and showroom appointments, he now chooses to stay in his office more often, keeping interactions brief and controlled.

His work has not disappeared, but it has become narrower and more effortful. He still sketches, still thinks in lines and textures, yet concentration slips away from him. He stares at a seam or a swatch and realizes several minutes have gone by without registering what he is doing. Decisions that used to come quickly now feel heavy and strangely threatening. He becomes irritated when others interrupt him, then immediately feels guilty for the sharpness in his voice. He notices that he is less patient with his staff, less available to his wife, and less like the man he used to be.

He also carries a constant sense of danger that does not match the quiet of his current life. He scans entrances in restaurants, checks locks more than once, and sits with his back to walls when he can. He says relaxation feels unfamiliar, almost irresponsible. Even when nothing is happening, he cannot fully let himself settle. His mood has thinned. He describes fewer moments of pleasure, less interest in the things that once animated him, and a persistent heaviness that makes the days feel long. He feels ashamed of how much the trauma has taken over his mind, especially because he believes he should be stronger after all these years.

What he expresses most, beneath the fear and vigilance, is grief. He mourns not only what happened to his wife but also the loss of the life they had before the injury entered it. He misses the ease between them, the ability to make plans without fear threading through every conversation. He loves her deeply and is often moved by small ordinary moments-a cup of tea she leaves for him, the sound of her voice in another room-but even these moments are shadowed by the knowledge of how quickly life can change. He lives now with a constant readiness for catastrophe, while trying to continue making clothes, keeping appointments, and moving through the world as if it still feels familiar.
